https://www.aol.co.uk/articles/nato-figh.text: Charlie Bradley Updated Sun, September 13, 2026 at 12:47 PM UTC 0 NATO fighter jets (Image: Getty) NATO fighter jets have been scrambled amid reports that a Russian drone was headed for Lithuania, but this was later confirmed to be a flock of birds. Flights were suspended at Vilnius Airport in the country's capital, and the Lithuanian National Crisis Management Centre issued a yellow alert for possible drone hazard in Vilnius, Trakai, and Elektrenai districts. The air alert has since been lifted by authorities. Vilmantas Vitkauskas, head of the National Crisis Management Center, said after the alert: "There is no threat, people can calm down. (...) In principle, the threat level has been eliminated." According to the Lithuanian Armed Forces, radars near Varna detected an object moving towards the Kaliningrad region. Authorities later confirmed: "Fighter jets carrying out a NATO air policing mission were deployed to inspect the object. They determined that the radar signals were a flock of birds." The Lithuanian military said earlier this week that drones aimed at Ukraine have landed in Lithuanian territory. Commander of the Armed Forces of Lithuania General Raimundas Vaikšnoras confirmed that Russian "Gerbera" drones were originally fired at Ukrainian cities before landing in Lithuania. Vilnius Airport (Image: Getty) Russia has issued numerous threats to Lithuania as the country continues to boost its defences amid fears it could be attacked by Moscow's forces. Just this week, former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev suggested wiping Lithuania "off the map." He said: "No one will come to their defence. Even if the place is reduced to scorched earth, no other country will go to war for them. And the well-known Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty - it will not be invoked, everyone recognises that. Because if it is invoked, it will be a global catastrophe, a planetary one. They are not fools. https://www.theargus.co.uk/news/26708296.text: Crime West Sussex Crime gang jailed for more than 100 years for drugs plot Crime West Sussex By Joseph Blakely Reporter Share 0 Comments 3 Skip to next photo 1 / 1 Show caption 1 / 1 Share 0 Comments This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. A crime gang who attempted to smuggle half a tonne of cocaine into Sussex has been sentenced to more than 100 years in prison. The 12 members of the organised crime group were jailed for plotting to bring 500kg of cocaine, worth an estimated £40 million, into the UK. The gang’s plot was foiled on August 19, 2024, when National Crime Agency officers intercepted the group as they landed 16 bales of cocaine on Medmerry Beach near Selsey. It is believed the drugs had been dropped into the sea a few days earlier by a crew aboard a container ship about 40 nautical miles south of the Needles, to the west of the Isle of Wight. The cocaine, with a purity of around 85 per cent, was packaged in waterproof bundles equipped with GPS trackers. The cocaine was pulled from the sea packaged in waterproof bales (Image: National Crime Agency) All 12 members were sentenced at Portsmouth Crown Court on November 5 and 6. The ringleaders were identified as Daniel Jamieson, 41, and Sam Brown, 33. Jamieson, of Heath Road, Ramsden Heath, Essex, was sentenced to 22 years in prison after being found guilty of conspiring to smuggle cocaine. He posed as a legitimate businessman and, under a false identity, acquired a maritime business and the inflatable boat used to recover the drugs. Brown, of Wykeham Street, Kirkdale, Liverpool, admitted the same charge and was jailed for 16 years and six months. Originally from Essex, Brown was said to have recruited others to join the conspiracy, including his friend Harry Kennedy, 38, who lived on the same street in Liverpool. Kennedy, who became involved the day before the drugs were landed, pleaded guilty to the same charge and was sentenced to nine years. Messages recovered during the investigation revealed that Brown and Kennedy were also involved in separate drug supply activities. Carl Powner, 62, of Park Road, Stoke-on-Trent, was sentenced to 13 years. He played a key role in the operation, recruiting drivers, sourcing equipment, and sailing out to recover the cocaine. Powner originally fled abroad but was arrested in Romania in May and extradited to the UK. He retrieved the drugs from the sea alongside Adil Nolan, 40, of Maureen Walk, Fazakerley, Liverpool, Nolan was sentenced to 11 years and three months after admitting conspiracy to smuggle cocaine. Oil rig worker David Paterson, 49, of Viking Way, Peterhead, near Aberdeen, had attempted an earlier retrieval of the drugs on August 17, but failed due to malfunctioning trackers. Paterson was convicted of conspiracy to smuggle cocaine and sentenced to 14 years. Lewis Watts, 37, of Toronto Road, Tilbury, Essex, was described as Jamieson’s "right-hand man," responsible for logistics and communication. He was in charge of a pre-paid credit card set up to fund the conspiracy, sourced equipment and acted as a go-between for conspirators in real life and online. He was sentenced to 14 years after being found guilty at trial of conspiracy to smuggle cocaine. Collectively the drugs weighed half a tonne and were worth an estimated £40 million (Image: National Crime Agency) A further five individuals, involved in the landing operation on Medmerry Beach, were convicted of assisting an organised crime group. Charlotte Blenman, 34, of Shelley Road East, Boscombe, Bournemouth, received a 20-month sentence suspended for two years. Roy Harmer, 46, of Chine Road, Bournemouth; Neil Pinchbeck, 43, of Pearce Road, Poole; Thomas Stewart, 40, of Carpenter Close, Peterborough; and Ricky Platt, 49, of Westby Road, Boscombe, each received 20-month prison sentences. Read more Traveller wins permission to keep mobile home after battle with council Fire-damaged convent site goes up for auction amid major housing plans Plans for hundreds of homes on edge of city withdrawn Jules Harriman, senior investigating officer at the NCA, said: "The main players from this conspiracy are facing very long periods behind bars. "Had their smuggling attempt worked, these toxic drugs would have brought misery and violence to many communities around the country. "The crime group responsible for supplying these offenders has lost their drugs and massive profits that can no longer be ploughed back into further offending. "Working with partners such as Border Force, the NCA will continue to do all it can to protect the public from the threat of Class A drugs." The NCA thanked Merseyside Police, West Mercia Police, Hampshire Police, and Sussex Police for their support during the investigation. Photograph: Eduardo Muñoz/Reuters View image in fullscreen Nusseibeh, as UAE ambassador to the UN, arriving to address the 80th general assembly in New York in September 2025. Photograph: Eduardo Muñoz/Reuters United Nations Interview ‘I’m no longer a UAE official’: UN hopeful Lana Nusseibeh tries to shake off Sudan record Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor The US and Russia’s candidate for secretary general is on a charm offensive. Can she overcome London’s resistance to her bid? Thu 26 Nov 2026 07.37 EST Last modified on Thu 26 Nov 2026 08.18 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google L ana Nusseibeh is in Britain this week, attempting to present herself as a potential future UN secretary general, and shift the focus from her past as a United Arab Emirates diplomat who denied the country’s role in arming a militia accused of war crimes and genocide in Sudan’s four-year civil war. It is a high-risk strategy that involves meeting ministers, MPs, academics and holding a public event with the UN Association. Labelled by many British NGOs and others as an apologist for war crimes, Nusseibeh is presenting herself as a skilled diplomat with the network to put the UN back at the centre of mediation, development and human rights. “These are very geopolitical times,” she said in an interview. “You need a geopolitical secretary general, because the fact is these geopolitical ruptures are not going away. These fissures in the international system are not going to dissolve any time soon.” View image in fullscreen Lana Nusseibeh in March, when she was the UAE’s minister of state. Photograph: Abdelhadi Ramahi/Reuters Nusseibeh had a setback last Friday, when three permanent members of the UN security council, China, France and the UK , all voted to “discourage” her candidature. The UN’s electoral system requires that she secure nine positive votes from the 15-strong security council, and no discouragement from the permanent five (P5) before being recommended to the UN general assembly. She has the backing of the US and Russia, and thinks her cause is not lost. “Sometimes, the use of the veto is tactical. Sometimes, it’s a holding position, sometimes it’s a leveraging position. There are a number of different theories”. The centre of the resistance to Nusseibeh’s candidacy is probably London, and specifically the Foreign Office, the penholder on Sudan at the UN, and this may explain the UK political blitz. When questioned about her role in Sudan, she asked that her candidacy be seen in the round, highlighting her role in forcing humanitarian aid into Gaza, her support for Afghan women and promoting interfaith tolerance. Sudanese diaspora and human rights groups denounce UAE nominee for UN top job Read more “Like every candidate, I come from somewhere, but the independence of the incoming secretary general is the key to their credibility. “I’ve taken a leave of absence from my role in [the] UAE government in order to independently campaign for this role. But I think that if I was secretary general, Sudan would be the litmus test of success for any incoming secretary because it’s such a horrific humanitarian crisis.” The war in Sudan, which erupted in April 2023 after a power struggle between the ​military and the Rapid Support Forces, has displaced more than 14 million people and created one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises. Multiple regional powers, including the UAE , have backed different local proxies since the beginning of the conflict in an attempt to win influence and strategic resources. The UAE has long been accused of supporting the RSF in Sudan, a charge repeatedly denied by Nusseibeh, who has publicly disputed the findings of UN investigators. A UN panel of experts suggested last month that the UAE had supplied crucial support to the RSF. Asked if she regretted dissembling during her time as a diplomat, by denying the UAE had armed the RSF, or her personal role in challenging the UN reports critical of the UAE, Nusseibeh said she regretted that “the Sudanese civil war had continued for so long”. View image in fullscreen Fighters who defected from the RSF gathered in western Omdurman, Sudan, earlier this month. Photograph: Marwan Ali/AP Nusseibeh added: “But I don’t think saying that is enough for the Sudanese people and the people in the surrounding countries where they’ve also felt the impact of this war, or for the victims of sexual violence and in this conflict, the atrocities committed in El Fasher without accountability, and the use of chemical weapons against the civilian population; all of these are a litany of suffering that has been inflicted on the Sudanese people.” Asked if the UAE had been supplying weapons to the RSF in a breach of a UN embargo, she replied: “I’m aware of the allegations. I haven’t read the last UN panel of experts report, but I’m not going to comment as I’m no longer a UAE official. In this campaign, I am a secretary general candidate. “As secretary general, I would fully back the findings of all UN panel of experts reports and I’m aware that I think several countries have been mentioned in various reports.”She later added: “I would call out countries that are supplying arms to any of the parties, including those in the RSF … this needs a process that requires accountability for atrocities that have been committed. That it needs to be a process primarily led by the Sudanese people.” UK and France believed to have vetoed UAE choice for UN secretary general Read more Nusseibeh said she was willing to take risks to mediate and to put UN values, expertise and its development toolkit at the centre of disputes. Her analysis of contemporary diplomacy was that the world had descended into a default setting of non-cooperation, and the UN needed to restate the case for collaboration between nations as being in the self-interest of everyone. The UN had been missing from too many conflicts, she argued, and she would set up a mediation board to try to use the full UN toolkit, ranging from confidence-building measures to development to secure peace. “What’s missing is this idea of a secretary general that is a strategist and a mediator-in-chief that is looking at the sort of the blips on the dashboard of conflict and saying, ‘How do we deploy to have maximum impact for most effective use of resource and cost?’ Because resources are not going up, they’re going down. I mean, we’re looking at, since 2010, 40% increase in military spending. So we’re using a lot of hard power as countries and systems to deter, but it’s not actually working.” That would require some prioritisation at the UN – it has 4,000 different open mandates. Her intelligence and skills as a diplomat are not in question. However, her track record over Sudan is. One critic said: “It is a very smart strategic play by the UAE that seeks autocratic capture, and then the asset-stripping of the UN and its standards. The UAE would end the UN’s role on climate. It would be a catastrophe.” The next security council vote is on Monday. By then some of the backmarkers may have dropped out of the race. The diplomats of the P5 may also be clearer on the flexibility of their mandates, in which case the papal conclave may finally produce white smoke.
